newsitem.title: MEXICO: Banco de Mexico net reserves fall, assets rise.
newsitem.headline: Banco de Mexico net reserves fall, assets rise.

text.p: Banco de Mexico said on Tuesday its international reserves as of Aug. 15 were $22.676 billion, compared to $22.726 billion on Aug. 8.
The central bank said that its net international assets as of the same date were $15.951 billion compared to $15.609 billion the week before.
The central bank said the increase of $342 million in net international assets during the period was due to:
--Net income from operations by the state oil company Pemex worth $461 million.
--Net outflows of foreign currency from operations with the federal government worth $142 million.

--A net gain of $23 million for a combination of factors including changes in the dollar value of non-dollar assets and liabilities held by the bank; net returns on interest rates and from trading of metals and securities; and net deposits in dollar accounts from commercial banks at the central bank.

Banco de Mexico said that between Aug. 8 and Aug. 15 the monetary base fell 1.875 billion pesos, mostly because of an increase in the seasonal demand of bills and coins and the payment of salaries in the first half of August.
In the same period, the government's balance at the central bank fell 8.326 billion pesos.

To neutralize the increase in liquidity resulting from lower deposits from the federal government and increased assets, the central bank intervened with a total of 7.165 billion pesos in the secondary money market.
The following tables detail Banco de Mexico's reserves and net domestic credit. All figures are in billions of pesos, unless otherwise indicated.
Aug. 8 Aug. 15
International Reserves
U.S. Dollars $22.726 bln $22.676 bln
Monetary Base 81.068 82.943
Net International Assets*
U.S. Dollars $15.609 bln $15.951 bln
Net Domestic Credit -41.096 -40.910
*Net International Assets are defined as gross international assets minus central bank liabilities with the IMF and assets of less than a six-month duration from other central banks.
((--Dan Trotta, Mexico City newsroom +525 728-9507))
